newsitem.title: MEXICO: Mexico's PRI said in anti-corruption campaign.
newsitem.headline: Mexico's PRI said in anti-corruption campaign.

text.p: Mexico's ruling party, long associated with corruption, said it was launching a major campaign against corruption just as the government was clamping down on offenders, newspapers reported on Sunday.

The Institutional Revolutionary Party (PRI), replete with government officials who ostentatiously live far beyond their means, will make the fight against corruption a major plank in the July 6 congressional elections, a top party leader said.

The party must have "scrupulously honest conduct with the public's money and in the decisions of the government," Roberto Campa Cifrian, PRI president for Mexico City told party leaders, according to the newspaper Uno Mas Uno.
The PRI has governed Mexico for 67 consecutive years.
At the same time, the attorney general's office said over the weekend that it has brought corruption charges against Andres Sigfrido Paz Paredes, former vice minister of tourism.

The newspaper La Cronica de Hoy reported on Sunday that the attorney general was investigating former Attorney General Antonio Lozano and one of his top investigators for misusing funds and possibly for seeking to trump up charges against the brother of former President Carlos Salinas de Gortari.

Last week, President Ernesto Zedillo lashed out at the foreign press and political analysts who continue to paint Mexico as a corrupt and autocratic regime, calling them pessimists out of step with the modern Mexico.

That was immediately followed by the publicised case against Paz Paredes, accused of awarding government contracts to a company in which his daughter is part owner, the government news agency Notimex reported.
The attorney general's office said legal action would be taken against Paz Paredes for "his probable responsibility in committing offences as a public servant."
La Cronica newspaper said the attorney general has opened an investigation of Lozano, who was the only opposition party member in Zedillo's cabinet until he was fired on Dec. 2.

La Cronica said the probe would focus on Lozano and Pablo Chapa Benzanilla, a special prosecutor who was fired along with Lozano, surrounding the mystery of a skeleton that was dug up on a ranch used by Raul Salinas de Gortari, the former president's brother.

In 1995, Lozano had Raul Salinas jailed for a 1994 political murder, and when the skeleton was unearthed last October, Lozano speculated publicly the remains belonged to a Salinas associate who allegedly was killed to cover up the original murder.

Forensics experts have since proved that theory wrong, saying the bones did not belong to Manuel Munoz Rocha, a PRI congressman who has been missing since shortly after the murder of PRI Secretary General Jose Francisco Ruiz Massieu.
But Lozano defended his actions in the case of the skeleton, telling reporters he was willing to cooperate with investigators regarding any doubts they had about the case.
